s: Vêdanîya is a Karman (one of the eight kinds)
q: The eight kinds of Karman are briefly the following: 1. Gñânâvaranîya (which acts as an obstruction to right knowledge); 2. Darsanâvaranîya (which acts as an obstruction to right faith); 3. Vêdanîya

s: Vêdanîya leads to experiencing pleasures (as one of two forms)
q: 3. Vêdanîya (which leads to experiencing pain or pleasure);

s: Vêdanîya leads to experiencing misery (as one of two forms)
q: 3. Vêdanîya (which leads to experiencing pain or pleasure);

s: Lêsyâ is a state of the soul (produced by Karman)
q: I shall deliver in due order the Lecture on Lêsyâ; hear the nature of the six Lêsyâs (produced by) Karman. (1)

s: black Lêsyâ is developed by man acting on the impulse of the five Âsravas (without the three Guptis and without ceasing to injure the six kinds of living beings)
q: A man who acts on the impulse of the five Âsravas, does not possess the three Guptis, has not ceased to injure the six (kinds of living beings), commits cruel acts, is wicked and violent, is afraid of no consequences, is mischievous and does not subdue his senses--a man of such habits develops the black Lêsyâ. (21, 22)

s: blue Lêsyâ is a lowest Lêsyâ
q: The black, blue, and grey Lêsyâs are the lowest Lêsyâs; through them the soul is brought into miserable courses of life. (56)

s: blue Lêsyâ has colour blue Asôka (also like the tail of the Kasha or lapis lazuli)
q: The blue Lêsyâ has the colour of the blue Asôka, the tail of the Kasha, or of lapis lazuli. (5)

s: blue Lêsyâ has taste pungent (infinitely more pungent than Trikatuka and Hastipippalî)
q: The taste of the blue Lêsyâ is infinitely more pungent than Trikatuka and Hastipippalî. (11)

s: blue Lêsyâ is developed by man characterized by envy, anger, want of self-control, ignorance, deceit, greed, hatred, wickedness, carelessness, and love of enjoyment (also pursues pleasures and sinful undertakings)
q: A man of the following qualities: envy, anger, want of self-control, ignorance, deceit, want of modesty, greed, hatred, wickedness, carelessness, love of enjoyment; a man who pursues pleasures and does not abstain from sinful undertakings, who is wicked and violent--a man of such habits develops the blue Lêsyâ. (23, 24)

s: grey Lêsyâ is a lowest Lêsyâ
q: The black, blue, and grey Lêsyâs are the lowest Lêsyâs; through them the soul is brought into miserable courses of life. (56)

s: grey Lêsyâ has colour flower of Atasî (also like the feathers of the Kôkila or collar of pigeons)
q: The grey Lêsyâ has the colour of the flower of Atasî, the feathers of the Kôkila, or the collar of pigeons. (6)

s: grey Lêsyâ has taste sour (infinitely sourer than unripe Mango and Kapittha)
q: The taste of grey Lêsyâ is infinitely sourer than that of unripe Mango and Kapittha. (12)

s: grey Lêsyâ is developed by dishonest, base, deceitful, heretical, hurtful, sinful, thieving, and jealous man (dishonest in words and acts)
q: A man who is dishonest in words and acts, who is base, not upright, a dissembler and deceiver, a heretic, a vile man, a talker of hurtful and sinful things, a thief, and full of jealousy--a man of such habits develops the grey Lêsyâ. (25, 26)

s: red Lêsyâ is a good Lêsyâ
q: The red, yellow, and white Lêsyâs are the good Lêsyâs; through them the soul is brought into happy courses of life. (57)

s: Lêsyâ has parts six types (black, blue, grey, red, yellow, and white)
q: 1. They are named in the following order: black, blue, grey, red, yellow, and white. (3)

s: red Lêsyâ has colour vermilion (also like the rising sun or bill of a parrot)
q: The red Lêsyâ has the colour of vermilion, the rising sun, or the bill of a parrot. (7)

s: red Lêsyâ has taste pleasant (infinitely more pleasant than ripe Mango and Kapittha)
q: The taste of red Lêsyâ is infinitely more pleasant than that of ripe Mango and Kapittha. (13)

s: red Lêsyâ is developed by humble, steadfast, disciplined, restrained, attentive, dutiful, and law-loving man (free from deceit and inquisitiveness)
q: A man who is humble, steadfast, free from deceit and inquisitiveness, well disciplined, restrained, attentive to his study and duties, who loves the Law and keeps it, who is afraid of forbidden things and strives after the highest good--a man of such habits develops the red Lêsyâ. (27, 28)

s: yellow Lêsyâ is a good Lêsyâ
q: The red, yellow, and white Lêsyâs are the good Lêsyâs; through them the soul is brought into happy courses of life. (57)

s: yellow Lêsyâ has colour orpiment (also like turmeric or flowers of Sana and Asana)
q: The yellow Lêsyâ has the colour of orpiment, turmeric, or the flowers of Sana and Asana. (8)

s: yellow Lêsyâ has taste better than excellent wine, liquors, honey, and Mairêyaka (infinitely better)
q: The taste of yellow Lêsyâ is infinitely better than that of excellent wine and various liquors, honey and Mairêyaka. (14)

s: yellow Lêsyâ is developed by calm, self-controlled, restrained, and sense-subduing man (with little anger, pride, deceit, and greed)
q: A man who has but little anger, pride, deceit, and greed, whose mind is at ease, who controls himself, who is attentive to his study and duties, who speaks but little, is calm, and subdues his senses--a man of such habits develops the yellow Lêsyâ. (29, 30)

s: white Lêsyâ is a good Lêsyâ
q: The red, yellow, and white Lêsyâs are the good Lêsyâs; through them the soul is brought into happy courses of life. (57)

s: white Lêsyâ has colour conch-shell (also like aṅka-stone, Kunda-flowers, flowing milk, silver, or a necklace of pearls)
q: The white Lêsyâ has the colour of a conch-shell, the aṅka-stone, Kunda-flowers, flowing milk, silver, or a necklace of pearls. (9)

s: white Lêsyâ has taste better than dates, grapes, milk, candied sugar, and pounded sugar (infinitely better)
q: The taste of white Lêsyâ is infinitely better than that of dates, grapes, milk, candied and pounded sugar. (15)

s: Lêsyâ has degrees three, nine, twenty-seven, eighty-one, or two hundred and forty-three
q: 6. The degrees of the Lêsyâs are three, or nine, or twenty-seven, or eighty-one, or two hundred and forty-three. (20)

s: white Lêsyâ is developed by calm, self-controlled, meditative, and sense-subduing man (meditating on Law and truth and practising the Samitis and Guptis)
q: A man who abstains from constant thinking about his misery and about sinful deeds, but engages in meditation on the Law and truth only, whose mind is at ease, who controls himself, who practises the Samitis and Guptis, whether he be still subject to passion or free from passion, is calm, and subdues his senses--a man of such habits develops the white Lêsyâ. (31, 32)

s: miserable courses of life are reached through black Lêsyâ (also through blue and grey Lêsyâs)
q: The black, blue, and grey Lêsyâs are the lowest Lêsyâs; through them the soul is brought into miserable courses of life. (56)

s: happy courses of life are reached through red Lêsyâ (also through yellow and white Lêsyâs)
q: The red, yellow, and white Lêsyâs are the good Lêsyâs; through them the soul is brought into happy courses of life. (57)

s: Lêsyâ has duration half a muhûrta to thirty-three Sâgarôpamâs plus one muhûrta (black Lêsyâ)
q: Half a muhûrta is the shortest, and thirty-three Sâgarôpamâs plus one muhûrta is the longest duration of the black Lêsyâ. (34)

s: Lêsyâ is joined to new existence (the soul is not born into a new existence in the first or last moment of conjunction)
q: In the first moment of these Lêsyâs when they are joined (with the soul), the latter is not born into a new existence. (58) In the last moment of all these Lêsyâs when they are joined (with the soul), the latter is not born into a new existence. (59)

s: Lêsyâ leads to new existence (while the last muhûrta is running and part of it remains)
q: While the last muhûrta is running and a part of it is still to come, the souls with their Lêsyâs developed, go to a new birth. (60)

s: Lêsyâ has varieties as many as there are Samayas in the innumerable Avasarpinîs and Utsarpinîs and countless worlds
q: 8. There are as many varieties of Lêsyâs as there are Samayas in the innumerable Avasarpinîs and Utsarpinîs, and as there are countless worlds. (33)

s: black Lêsyâ is a lowest Lêsyâ
q: The black, blue, and grey Lêsyâs are the lowest Lêsyâs; through them the soul is brought into miserable courses of life. (56)

s: black Lêsyâ has colour rain-cloud (also like a buffalo's horn, Rishtaka, or the eye of the wagtail)
q: The black Lêsyâ has the colour of a rain-cloud, a buffalo's horn, (the fruit of) Rishtaka, or the eye of the wagtail. (4)

s: black Lêsyâ has taste bitter (infinitely more bitter than Tumbaka, Nimb-tree, or Rôhinî)
q: 3. The taste of the black Lêsyâ is infinitely more bitter than that of Tumbaka, (the fruit of the) Nimb-tree, or of Rôhinî. (10)

s: black Lêsyâ has smell worse than the corpse of a cow, dog, or snake (infinitely worse)
q: The smell of the bad Lêsyâs (viz. the three first) is infinitely worse than that of the corpse of a cow, dog, or snake. (16)

s: black Lêsyâ has touch worse than a saw, the tongue of a cow, or leaf of the Teak tree (infinitely worse)
q: 5. The touch of the bad Lêsyâs is infinitely worse than that of a saw, the tongue of a cow, or leaf of the Teak tree. (18)

s: monks is a Sramana
q: The Houseless Monk.

s: Sramana abstains from desire
q: A restrained monk should abstain from killing, lying, stealing, carnal intercourse, from desire, love, and greed. (3)

s: Sramana abstains from love
q: A restrained monk should abstain from killing, lying, stealing, carnal intercourse, from desire, love, and greed. (3)

s: Sramana abstains from greed
q: A restrained monk should abstain from killing, lying, stealing, carnal intercourse, from desire, love, and greed. (3)

s: Sramana does not long for house (even in his thoughts; pleasant and decorated)
q: Even in his thoughts a monk should not long for a pleasant painted house filled with the fragrance of garlands and frankincense, secured by doors, and decorated with a white ceiling-cloth. (4)

s: house is filled with fragrance of garlands and frankincense (pleasant painted house)
q: Even in his thoughts a monk should not long for a pleasant painted house filled with the fragrance of garlands and frankincense, secured by doors, and decorated with a white ceiling-cloth. (4)

s: house is secured by doors
q: Even in his thoughts a monk should not long for a pleasant painted house filled with the fragrance of garlands and frankincense, secured by doors, and decorated with a white ceiling-cloth. (4)

s: house is decorated with white ceiling-cloth
q: Even in his thoughts a monk should not long for a pleasant painted house filled with the fragrance of garlands and frankincense, secured by doors, and decorated with a white ceiling-cloth. (4)

s: house increases desire and passion (by making restraint of the senses difficult)
q: For in such a dwelling a monk will find it difficult to prevent his senses from increased desire and passion. (5)

s: Sramana lives in burial-place (contentedly)
q: He should be content to live on a burial-place, in a deserted house, below a tree, in solitude, or in a place which had been prepared for the sake of somebody else. (6)

s: Sramana lives below tree (contentedly)
q: He should be content to live on a burial-place, in a deserted house, below a tree, in solitude, or in a place which had been prepared for the sake of somebody else. (6)

s: Sramana follows road (the road shown by the wise ones)
q: Learn from me, with attentive minds, the road shown by the wise ones, which leads a monk who follows it, to the end of all misery. (1)

s: Sramana lives in solitude (contentedly)
q: He should be content to live on a burial-place, in a deserted house, below a tree, in solitude, or in a place which had been prepared for the sake of somebody else. (6)

s: Sramana is a well-controlled
q: A well-controlled monk should live in a pure place, which is not too much crowded, and where no women live. (7)

s: Sramana lives in pure place (not too much crowded and where no women live)
q: A well-controlled monk should live in a pure place, which is not too much crowded, and where no women live. (7)

s: Sramana does not build house (nor cause others to erect one)
q: He should not build a house, nor cause others to erect one; for many living beings both movable and immovable, both subtile and gross, are seen to be killed when a house is being built; therefore a monk should abstain from building a house. (8, 9)

s: house kills Living Beings (when being built; movable and immovable, subtile and gross)
q: He should not build a house, nor cause others to erect one; for many living beings both movable and immovable, both subtile and gross, are seen to be killed when a house is being built; therefore a monk should abstain from building a house. (8, 9)

s: Sramana does not cook food and drink (nor cause another to cook; out of compassion for living beings)
q: The same holds good with the cooking of food and drink, or with one's causing them to be cooked. Out of compassion for living beings one should not cook nor cause another to cook. (10)

s: food and drink destroys Living Beings (beings living in water, corn, or in earth and wood)
q: Beings which live in water, corn, or in earth and wood, are destroyed in food and drink; therefore a monk should cause nobody to cook. (11)

s: Sramana does not light fire
q: There is nothing so dangerous as fire, for it spreads in all directions and is able to destroy many beings; one should therefore not light a fire. (12)

s: fire destroys Living Beings (by spreading in all directions)
q: There is nothing so dangerous as fire, for it spreads in all directions and is able to destroy many beings; one should therefore not light a fire. (12)

s: Sramana does not long for gold and silver (even in his thoughts)
q: Even in his thoughts a monk should not long for gold and silver; indifferent alike to dirt and gold he abstains from buying and selling. (13)

s: Sramana takes Pravragyâ (after giving up life in a house)
q: Giving up the life in a house, and taking Pravragyâ, a sage should know and renounce those attachments which take hold of men. (2)

s: Sramana abstains from buying and selling (indifferent alike to dirt and gold)
q: Even in his thoughts a monk should not long for gold and silver; indifferent alike to dirt and gold he abstains from buying and selling. (13)

s: buying and selling is a great sin
q: A monk who is to live on alms, should beg and not buy; buying and selling is a great sin; but to live on alms is benefitting. (15)

s: Sramana does not engage in buying and selling (a monk is not to engage in it)
q: If he buys, he becomes a buyer; if he sells, he becomes a merchant; a monk is not to engage in buying and selling. (14)

s: Sramana lives on alms (by begging rather than buying)
q: A monk who is to live on alms, should beg and not buy; buying and selling is a great sin; but to live on alms is benefitting. (15)

s: Sramana begs alms (in small parts according to the Sûtras and so as to avoid faults)
q: He should collect his alms in small parts according to the Sûtras and so as to avoid faults; a monk should contentedly go on his begging-tour, whether he get alms or not. (16)

s: Sramana goes on begging-tour (contentedly, whether he gets alms or not)
q: He should collect his alms in small parts according to the Sûtras and so as to avoid faults; a monk should contentedly go on his begging-tour, whether he get alms or not. (16)

s: Sramana eats food and drink (for sustenance of life, not for pleasant taste)
q: A great sage should not eat for the sake of the pleasant taste (of the food) but for the sustenance of life, being not dainty nor eager for good fare, restraining his tongue, and being without cupidity. (17)

s: Sramana restrains tongue (without cupidity and not eager for good fare)
q: A great sage should not eat for the sake of the pleasant taste (of the food) but for the sustenance of life, being not dainty nor eager for good fare, restraining his tongue, and being without cupidity. (17)

s: Sramana does not desire flowers (even in his thoughts; to be presented with them)
q: Even in his thoughts he should not desire to be presented with flowers, to be offered a seat, to be eloquently greeted, or to be offered presents, or to get a magnificent welcome and treatment. (18)

s: Sramana does not desire seat (even in his thoughts; to be offered one)
q: Even in his thoughts he should not desire to be presented with flowers, to be offered a seat, to be eloquently greeted, or to be offered presents, or to get a magnificent welcome and treatment. (18)

s: Sramana renounces attachments (after taking Pravragyâ)
q: Giving up the life in a house, and taking Pravragyâ, a sage should know and renounce those attachments which take hold of men. (2)

s: Sramana does not desire presents (even in his thoughts; to be offered them)
q: Even in his thoughts he should not desire to be presented with flowers, to be offered a seat, to be eloquently greeted, or to be offered presents, or to get a magnificent welcome and treatment. (18)

s: Sramana does not desire welcome and treatment (even in his thoughts; magnificent)
q: Even in his thoughts he should not desire to be presented with flowers, to be offered a seat, to be eloquently greeted, or to be offered presents, or to get a magnificent welcome and treatment. (18)

s: Sramana meditates on true things (only)
q: He should meditate on true things only, committing no sins and having no property; he should walk about careless of his body till his end arrives. 09)

s: Sramana has no property (while meditating on true things and committing no sins)
q: He should meditate on true things only, committing no sins and having no property; he should walk about careless of his body till his end arrives. 09)

s: Sramana is careless of human body (until his end arrives)
q: He should meditate on true things only, committing no sins and having no property; he should walk about careless of his body till his end arrives. 09)

s: Sramana rejects food and drink (when the time of death arrives)
q: Rejecting food when the time of his death arrives, and leaving the human body, he becomes his own master, and is liberated from misery. (20)

s: Sramana leaves human body (when the time of death arrives)
q: Rejecting food when the time of his death arrives, and leaving the human body, he becomes his own master, and is liberated from misery. (20)

s: Sramana is liberated from misery (after leaving the human body)
q: Rejecting food when the time of his death arrives, and leaving the human body, he becomes his own master, and is liberated from misery. (20)

s: Sramana is without property
q: Without property, without egoism, free from passions and the Âsravas, he obtains absolute knowledge, and reaches eternal beatitude. (21)

q: Without property, without egoism, free from passions and the Âsravas, he obtains absolute knowledge, and reaches eternal beatitude. (21)

q: The Living Beings and the Things without life make up this world (Lôka); but the space where only Things without life are found is called the Non-world (Alôka). (2)

q: The Living Beings and the Things without life will be described with reference to 1. substance, 2. place, 3. time, and 4. development. (3)

q: With regard to the continuous flow (or development of a thing) it is without beginning and without end; but with regard to its existence (as an individual thing) it has both a beginning and an end. (13)

s: Circle of Births is exited by those who love the creed of the Ginas (who piously practise it)
q: Those who love the creed of the Ginas and piously practise it, will be pure and free from the soil (of passions), and will (in due time) get out of the Circle of Births. (259)

s: Bhâvanâs lead to bad births (Kandarpa-, Abhiyôgika-, Kilvisha-, Môha-, and Asuratva-Bhâvanâs)

s: Gñâtri(putra) delivered Thirty-six Lectures of the Uttarâdhyayana (the enlightened and liberated author)
q: The enlightened and liberated Gñâtri(putra) has thus delivered Thirty-six Lectures of the Uttarâdhyayana, which the pious approve of. (267)

q: This place, by nature pure, consisting of white gold, resembles in form an open umbrella, as has been said by the best of Ginas. (61)

s: Sramana practises tapas (penance, self-restraint, and self-control)
q: Once he saw pass there a restrained Sramana, who practised penance, self-restraint, and self-control, who was full of virtues, and a very mine of good qualities.

s: the monastic order has duties five great vows (difficult to perform)
q: Son, difficult to perform, are the duties of a Sramana; a monk must possess thousands of virtues.

s: five great vows include nonviolence (abstention from injury to living beings throughout life)
q: Impartiality towards all beings in the world, whether friends or enemies, and abstention from injury to living beings throughout the whole life: this is a difficult duty.

s: five great vows include truthfulness (abstention from falsehood and speaking wholesome truth)
q: To be never careless in abstaining from falsehood, and to be always careful to speak wholesome truth: this is a difficult duty.

s: five great vows include non-taking (abstention from taking what is not given)
q: To abstain from taking of what is not given, even of a toothpick, &c.; and to accept only alms free from faults: this is a difficult duty.

s: five great vows include chastity (abstention from unchastity)
q: To abstain from unchastity after one has tasted sensual pleasures, and to keep the severe vow of chastity: this is a very difficult duty.

s: five great vows include non-possession (giving up claims on wealth, corn, and servants)
q: To give up all claims on wealth, corn, and servants, to abstain from all undertakings, and not to own anything: this is a very difficult duty.

s: Balasrî seeks entry into the monastic order (after understanding the five great vows and suffering in hell and animal existence)
q: 'I have learned the five great vows; (I know) the suffering (that awaits the sinner) in hell or in an existence as a brute; I have ceased to take delight in the large ocean (of the Samsâra); therefore, O mother, allow me to enter the order.

s: Balasrî rejects pleasures (not delighted with them)
q: Being not delighted with pleasures, but devoted to self-control, he went to his father and mother, and spoke as follows:

s: pleasures are like Kimpâka-fruit (their consequences are painful)
q: As the effect of Kimpâka-fruit is anything but good, so the effect of pleasures enjoyed is anything but good.

s: body is a transitory residence (impure and a miserable vessel of suffering)
q: This body is not permanent, it is impure and of impure origin; it is but a transitory residence (of the soul) and a miserable vessel of suffering.

s: misery characterizes Samsâra (birth, old age, disease, and death are misery)
q: Birth is misery, old age is misery, and so are disease and death, and ah, nothing but misery is the Samsâra, in which men suffer distress.

s: Samsâra is a ocean (large and full of dangers)
q: I have ceased to take delight in the large ocean (of the Samsâra)

s: Samsâra contains the flood of old age and death (a wilderness of old age and death)
q: In the Samsâra, which is a mine of dangers and a wilderness of old age and death, I have undergone dreadful births and deaths.

s: hell causes misery (more painful than suffering in the human world)
q: O father, infinitely more painful is the suffering in hell than any suffering in the world of men.

s: former birth is recalled by Balasrî (upon seeing the Sramana)
q: While he looked at the saint, and his mind became pure, the remembrance of his former birth carne upon him as he was plunged in doubt.

s: former birth included Sramana (Balasrî had been a Sramana)
q: When the remembrance of his former birth came upon the illustrious Mrigâputra, he remembered his previous birth and his having been then a Sramana.

s: Mrigâputra's renunciation includes property (giving them up entirely)
q: With his parents' permission he gave up all his property.

s: Mrigâputra's renunciation includes family and relations (giving up friends, wives, sons, and relations)
q: His power and wealth, his friends, wives, sons, and relations he gave up as if he shook off the dust from his feet, and then he went forth.

s: Mrigâputra's renunciation renounces his power and wealth, his friends, wives, sons, and relations
q: His power and wealth, his friends, wives, sons, and relations he gave up as if he shook off the dust from his feet, and then he went forth.

s: Sramana observes five great vows (after going forth)
q: He observed the five great vows, practised the five Samitis, and was protected by the three Guptis; he exerted himself to do mental as well as bodily penance.

s: Sramana practises five Samitis (after going forth)
q: He observed the five great vows, practised the five Samitis, and was protected by the three Guptis; he exerted himself to do mental as well as bodily penance.

s: Sramana is protected by Guptis
q: He observed the five great vows, practised the five Samitis, and was protected by the three Guptis; he exerted himself to do mental as well as bodily penance.

s: Sramana is without property (without property and ownership)
q: He was without property, without egoism, without attachment, without conceit, impartial towards all beings, whether they move or not.

s: Sramana is indifferent to success and failure (in begging)
q: He was indifferent to success or failure (in begging), to happiness and misery, to life and death, to blame and praise, to honour and insult.

s: Sramana prevents Karman (preventing influx through all bad channels)
q: He prevented the influx of Karman (âsrava) through all bad channels; by meditating upon himself he obtained praiseworthy self-purification and sacred knowledge.

s: Karman has influx bad channels (prevented by the Sramana)
q: He prevented the influx of Karman (âsrava) through all bad channels; by meditating upon himself he obtained praiseworthy self-purification and sacred knowledge.

s: Sramana reaches Nirvâna (after many years of practice and monthly fasting)
q: Thus he thoroughly purified himself by knowledge, right conduct, faith, penance, and pure meditations, and after having lived many years as a Sramana, he reached perfection after breaking his fast once only every month.

s: Mrigâputra's liberation is famous in three worlds (as the result of austerities)
q: When you have heard the words of the illustrious and famous son of Mrigâ, his perfect practise of austerities, and his liberation, famous in the three worlds

s: Balasrî is a crown-prince (darling of his father and mother; future lord of ascetics)
q: Their son Balasrî, also known as Mrigâputra (i.e. son of Mrigâ), the darling of his father and mother, was crown-prince, a (future) lord of ascetics.

s: Mrigâputra's liberation is led by Law (to the great happiness of Nirvâna)
q: you will bear the excellent and pleasant yoke of the Law that leads to the great happiness of Nirvâna.

s: Law leads to Nirvâna (excellent and pleasant yoke)
q: you will bear the excellent and pleasant yoke of the Law that leads to the great happiness of Nirvâna.

s: animals lives in forest (by itself)
q: As a wild animal by itself roams about in the woods, thus I shall practise the Law by controlling myself and doing penance.

s: animals gets food and drink (in woods and lakes when healthy)
q: When it is in perfect health, it will roam about in woods and on (the shores of) lakes in search of food and drink.

s: animals is like Sramana (in roaming, living in many places, and obtaining food)
q: In the same way a pious monk goes to many places and walks about just as the animals, but afterwards he goes to the upper regions.

s: the flood of old age and death endanger world (the whole world is as if on fire)
q: so when the whole world is on fire, as it were, by old age and death, I shall save my Self, if you will permit me.

s: Balasrî is also known as Mrigâputra
q: Their son Balasrî, also known as Mrigâputra (i.e. son of Mrigâ), the darling of his father and mother, was crown-prince, a (future) lord of ascetics.

s: Balasrî is son of Mrigâ
q: Their son Balasrî, also known as Mrigâputra (i.e. son of Mrigâ), the darling of his father and mother, was crown-prince, a (future) lord of ascetics.

s: Balasrî resides in Nandana (palace)
q: In his palace Nandana he dallied with his wives, like the god Dôgundaga, always happy in his mind.

s: Sramana is a ascetic (restrained and virtuous)
q: Once he saw pass there a restrained Sramana, who practised penance, self-restraint, and self-control, who was full of virtues, and a very mine of good qualities.

s: The Great Duty of the Nirgranthas is a sermon (great and extensive)
q: Thus the austere and calm, great ascetic and great sage who kept great vows and possessed great fame, preached at great length this great sermon: the great duty of the Nirgranthas. (53)
